RESIDENTIAL PURCHASE AGREEMENT
Prepared for Pat Morgan · Jordan Lee

PARTIES AND PROPERTY
This is a residential purchase agreement between Pat Morgan ("Seller") and Jordan Lee ("Buyer") for the property at 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814, for a purchase price of $750,000.

TRANSFER DISCLOSURE STATEMENT REQUIREMENT
Except for the specific exemptions below, California law requires the seller of single-family residential property to deliver to a prospective buyer a completed written Transfer Disclosure Statement, for any transfer by sale, exchange, real property sales contract, lease with an option to purchase, other option to purchase, or ground lease coupled with improvements. Any waiver of this requirement is void as against public policy. The following transfers are specifically exempted from this requirement: transfers pursuant to court order (including probate-court sales, writ-of-execution sales, foreclosure sales, bankruptcy-trustee transfers, eminent domain, and decree-of-specific-performance sales); sales or transfers by a fiduciary in the administration of a trust, guardianship, conservatorship, or decedent's estate (with an exception to this exemption if the trustee is a natural person who is also a former owner or was a recent occupant of the property); transfers from one co-owner to one or more other co-owners; transfers to a spouse or to a person in the transferor's line of consanguinity; transfers between spouses resulting from a dissolution or legal-separation judgment or an incidental property settlement agreement; and sales, transfers, or exchanges to or from a governmental entity.

  Known gap: This exemption list is longer and more specific than commonly assumed — the decedent's-estate fiduciary exemption in particular has its own built-in exception that's easy to miss on a first read. This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of how one jurisdiction defines residential transfer-disclosure exemptions — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific residential purchase; real estate disclosure requirements vary enormously by state. The statute's scope term is "single-family residential property," which is narrower-sounding than the "one to four dwelling units" language this same body of California disclosure law uses elsewhere (for example, in the liquidated-damages and Megan's Law notice statutes cited elsewhere in this document) — this document does not resolve or equate those two scope terms for any specific transaction. The two citations to § 1102 below are subsections of the same statutory section; the six citations to § 1102.2 are also subsections of the same statutory section as each other, and § 1102.2 is a genuinely separate, independent section from § 1102.

WHAT THE DISCLOSURE STATEMENT MUST COVER
The Transfer Disclosure Statement is set forth in, and must be made on a copy of, a specific statutory disclosure form. The disclosure requirement covers any fact materially affecting the value and desirability of the property, including the physical conditions of the property and previously received reports of physical inspections. Delivery of the disclosure statement cannot be waived in an "as is" sale. The form has a specific three-part structure: Sections I and II, and — if the seller is represented by an agent in the transaction — also Section III (the agent's own inspection disclosure).

DISCLOSURE TIMING AND BUYER'S RIGHT TO TERMINATE
In the case of a sale, the seller must deliver the completed Transfer Disclosure Statement to the prospective buyer as soon as practicable before transfer of title. If any disclosure, or a material amendment to a disclosure, is delivered after the buyer's offer to purchase has already been executed, the buyer has three days after delivery in person, five days after delivery by mail, or five days after delivery of an electronic record (where the parties have agreed to conduct the transaction electronically) to terminate the offer, by delivering written notice of termination to the seller or the seller's agent. Noncompliance with this disclosure article does not by itself invalidate the transfer, but a person who willfully or negligently violates or fails to perform any duty under this article is liable to the buyer for the buyer's actual damages.

NATURAL HAZARD DISCLOSURE
Separately from the Transfer Disclosure Statement, California law requires a distinct Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement whenever the seller or the seller's agent is required by other law to disclose the property's location within a hazard zone. This statement must disclose, as its own itemized categories: whether the property lies within a special flood hazard area (FEMA Zone "A" or "V"); an area of potential flooding shown on a dam-failure inundation map; a high or very-high fire hazard severity zone (which also carries its own vegetation-maintenance requirement for the owner); a wildland area that may contain substantial forest-fire risks and hazards (which also carries its own maintenance requirement for the owner, and a statement that the state is not responsible for fire protection to structures there absent a specific cooperative agreement); an earthquake fault zone; and a seismic hazard zone (landslide or liquefaction). The statement itself says this information is not a warranty, though prospective buyers may rely on it in deciding whether and on what terms to buy. Any waiver of these natural-hazard disclosure requirements is void as against public policy. Separately, for a home constructed before January 1, 2010 and located in a high or very-high fire hazard severity zone, the seller must provide an additional, specific wildfire-hardening disclosure notice, in statutorily specified language.

MELLO-ROOS / SPECIAL TAX NOTICE DELIVERY
If 123 Main St., Sacramento, CA 95814 is subject to a special tax lien of the kind described in the Mello-Roos disclosure provisions below, Seller shall deliver to Buyer any Notice of Special Tax or other disclosure notice required by those provisions before Buyer signs a contract to purchase or a deposit receipt for the property, separately from the Transfer Disclosure Statement and Natural Hazard Disclosure Statement referenced elsewhere in this agreement.

NOTICE OF SPECIAL TAX — NEW-SUBDIVISION SALES
Where a lot, parcel, or unit of a subdivision is subject to a special tax levied under the Mello-Roos Community Facilities Act of 1982, California law bars the subdivider, or the subdivider's agent or representative, from selling the lot, parcel, or unit, or leasing it for more than five years, or permitting a prospective purchaser to sign a contract of purchase or a deposit receipt, until that purchaser has been furnished with, and has signed, a written notice in a statutorily specified form. The notice must carry the heading "NOTICE OF SPECIAL TAX" in type no smaller than 8-point type, and the statutory form itself states that the property is subject to a special tax in addition to regular property taxes and other charges, that the tax is imposed because the property is part of a new development, and that if the tax is not paid when due each year the property may be foreclosed upon and sold. "Subdivision" for this purpose means improved or unimproved land divided, or proposed to be divided, into two or more lots, parcels, or units for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, and by statutory definition includes a condominium project, a community apartment project, a stock cooperative, and a limited-equity housing cooperative.

SPECIAL TAX DISCLOSURE — GENERAL RESIDENTIAL RESALES
Separately from the subdivider's notice obligation described above, a distinct provision of California's residential Transfer Disclosure Statement article applies to a sale of real property that is subject to that article generally, where the property is subject to a continuing lien securing a special tax levied under the Mello-Roos Community Facilities Act of 1982 (among other listed lien types), and where a notice is not otherwise required under the subdivider-notice statute above. In that situation, in addition to any other disclosure required by the Transfer Disclosure Statement article, the seller must make a good faith effort to obtain a disclosure notice concerning the special tax from each local agency that levies it, and must deliver that notice, or those notices, to the prospective buyer, as long as the local agency makes the notice available.

After receiving the notice, the buyer has three days after personal delivery, or five days after delivery by deposit in the mail, to terminate the purchase agreement or deposit receipt, by delivering written notice of that termination to the owner, subdivider, or agent.

Where a lot, parcel, or unit of a subdivision is subject to a special tax levied under the Mello-Roos Community Facilities Act of 1982, California law bars the subdivider, or the subdivider's agent or representative, from selling the lot, parcel, or unit, or leasing it for more than five years, or permitting a prospective purchaser to sign a contract of purchase or a deposit receipt, until that purchaser has been furnished with, and has signed, a written notice in a statutorily specified form. The notice must carry the heading "NOTICE OF SPECIAL TAX" in type no smaller than 8-point type, and the statutory form itself states that the property is subject to a special tax in addition to regular property taxes and other charges, that the tax is imposed because the property is part of a new development, and that if the tax is not paid when due each year the property may be foreclosed upon and sold. "Subdivision" for this purpose means improved or unimproved land divided, or proposed to be divided, into two or more lots, parcels, or units for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, and by statutory definition includes a condominium project, a community apartment project, a stock cooperative, and a limited-equity housing cooperative.

It is imposed on this property because it is a new development, and is not necessarily imposed generally upon property outside of this new development. If you fail to pay this tax when due each year, the property may be foreclosed upon and sold. The tax is used to provide public facilities or services that are likely to particularly benefit the property.

citations.cite: California Government Code, statutory definition of 'subdivision'
citations.quote: “Subdivision,” as used in subdivision (a), means improved or unimproved land that is divided or proposed to be divided for the purpose of sale, lease, or financing, whether immediate or future, into two or more lots, parcels, or units and includes a condominium project, as defined by Section 4125 or 6542 of the Civil Code, a community apartment project, a stock cooperative, and a limited-equity housing cooperative, as defined in Sections 11004, 11003.2, and 11003.4, respectively, of the Business and Professions Code.
